title: Zorevunersen in Children and Adolescents with Dravet Syndrome
breakthrough: Zorevunersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that up-regulates NaV1.1 sodium channels, addressing the SCN1A haploinsufficiency that causes most Dravet syndrome. Across two phase 1-2a open-label multicentre studies (MONARCH and ADMIRAL) and their extensions, 81 patients aged 2 to 18 on standard antiseizure medication were enrolled from 2020 to 2023, with 75 continuing in extension for up to three years. Patients given 70 mg intrathecally in the phase 1-2a studies followed by up to 45 mg in extension had a median reduction in convulsive-seizure frequency ranging from 58.8% to 90.9% across successive one-month intervals over the first 20 months of extension, with improvements in quality of life and functioning reported by both clinicians and caregivers.
impact: The first antisense approach aimed at the genetic cause of a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy rather than at the seizures it produces, and the cognitive and behavioural signal is what makes the disease-modification hypothesis worth testing.
practical: Understand the evidence stage before offering this: these are open-label phase 1-2a studies with no control arm, and the authors describe zorevunersen as a *potential* disease-modifying treatment pending further development. Quote the range, not the ceiling — a median reduction between 59% and 91% depending on the interval is the honest figure. Delivery is intrathecal and repeated, so a care pathway has to accommodate serial lumbar punctures in a child with a severe epilepsy.
link: NEJM — zorevunersen in children and adolescents with Dravet syndrome

verify.status: corrected — trial phase, and the seizure figure was the best interval rather than the result
verify.note: Real and correctly identified: NEJMoa2506295, PMID 41780062, zorevunersen targeting SCN1A haploinsufficiency to up-regulate NaV1.1. THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) PHASE: the submission implies a definitive trial. These are two phase 1-2a OPEN-LABEL studies (MONARCH and ADMIRAL) plus extensions, 81 patients enrolled, 75 continuing — no control group, so the effect size cannot be separated from natural history and concomitant therapy. (2) The submission quotes 'up to a 91% reduction in monthly seizure frequency'. The reported result is a median change ranging from −58.82% to −90.91% across one-month intervals; citing only the ceiling is the most favourable possible reading. Range given instead. (3) 'Disease-modifying' is softened to potential, which is the paper's own wording. The submission's practical point about serial lumbar punctures is right and kept; monitoring of CSF protein specifically could not be confirmed and is not asserted.

title: Routine Gastric Residual Volume Measurement in Critically Ill Children (GASTRIC-PICU)
breakthrough: A multicentre, open-label, non-inferiority randomised trial across 23 PICUs in the United Kingdom, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Switzerland enrolled 4,700 children aged 0 to 16 starting enteral feeds while requiring invasive ventilation, between June 2023 and December 2025. Omitting routine gastric residual volume assessment was non-inferior to checking at least every 6 hours for survival and days alive without mechanical ventilation at 30 days (median 25 days, IQR 21 to 27, in both groups). The proportion of energy requirements met by 72 hours was 80.3% without routine checks versus 76.8% with them.
impact: A 4,700-child trial is decisive for a practice that was never based on evidence in the first place. Aspirating and measuring gastric contents every few hours was inherited ritual, and the trial shows nothing is lost by stopping.
practical: Stop routine six-hourly residual checks in the ventilated child who is feeding, and monitor clinically instead — abdominal distension, vomiting, discomfort. Keep expectations calibrated: the nutritional gain was real but modest, about 3.5 percentage points of energy target by 72 hours, and the primary result is non-inferiority on survival and ventilator-free days rather than a demonstrated improvement in outcome.
link: JAMA — gastric residual volume assessment in critically ill children: the GASTRIC-PICU randomized clinical trial

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, design and effect size clarified
verify.note: Verified: JAMA, 23 PICUs across the UK, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Switzerland, 4,700 children aged 0-16, June 2023 to December 2025, non-inferiority open-label design, no routine GRV non-inferior for survival and ventilator-free days at 30 days (median 25 days both groups), energy targets 80.3% versus 76.8% at 72 hours. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission says omission 'resulted in earlier delivery of target enteral nutrition with no increase in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) or aspiration events'. The measured nutritional difference is 3.5 percentage points of energy target by 72 hours — real but not the substantial acceleration implied — and VAP and aspiration as specifically reported outcomes could not be confirmed, so they are not asserted; the confirmed primary outcome is stated instead. (2) The non-inferiority design was missing and matters: this shows nothing is lost, not that outcomes improve. Trial size added, since 4,700 children is the reason this settles the question.

title: Fremanezumab for Preventive Treatment of Episodic Migraine in Children and Adolescents (SPACE)
breakthrough: SPACE is the first phase 3 trial of an anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody in children. 237 patients aged 6 to 17 with episodic migraine were randomised to monthly fremanezumab 120 mg, 220 mg or placebo. Both doses produced greater reductions in monthly migraine days and higher response rates than placebo over 3 months, with fewer days of moderate-to-severe headache and reduced acute migraine medication use. Safety was consistent with adult experience and no new signals emerged. The FDA had already expanded the indication to paediatric episodic migraine on monthly dosing, based on earlier SPACE results.
impact: Fills a real gap. Paediatric migraine prophylaxis has rested on drugs borrowed from adults with poor tolerability, and the CHAMP trial had previously shown topiramate and amitriptyline no better than placebo in this age group.
practical: A monthly subcutaneous injection avoids the daily adherence problem and the cognitive and weight effects that make topiramate hard to sustain in a school-age child. Get the drug class right: fremanezumab is an anti-CGRP monoclonal ANTIBODY, not a CGRP receptor antagonist — the gepants are the antagonists, they are oral, and they have not been established in this population.
link: NEJM / SPACE — fremanezumab for prevention of episodic migraine in children and adolescents

verify.status: matched with corrections — drug class mislabelled, details added
verify.note: Verified: SPACE, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3, 237 patients aged 6-17, fremanezumab 120 mg and 220 mg monthly, published in NEJM online 14 January 2026, first phase 3 evidence for an anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody in children, safety consistent with adults. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) TERMINOLOGY: the submission's guideline-impact line says the trial 'Established CGRP antagonists as a recommended, evidence-based preventive class'. Fremanezumab is a monoclonal antibody against CGRP, not a CGRP receptor antagonist — the gepants are the antagonists and were not studied here. Conflating them would have a clinician reach for the wrong drug. (2) The submission presents guideline incorporation as the regulatory consequence; what is confirmed is that the FDA had already expanded the paediatric indication based on earlier SPACE data, which is the stronger and more actionable fact. Added n, ages and doses, and the CHAMP context that explains why this gap existed.

title: Two-Year Crinecerfont Data in Pediatric Classic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAHtalyst Pediatric)
journal: Presented at the Pediatric Endocrine Society 2026 and ENDO 2026
breakthrough: Crinecerfont is an oral corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 receptor antagonist. In the open-label extension of the phase 3 CAHtalyst Pediatric study, 86 participants aged 4 to 17 completing up to two years of treatment showed durable reductions in ACTH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone while achieving lower, more physiologic glucocorticoid doses. Growth measures were reported separately at ENDO 2026.
impact: Breaks the central compromise of classic CAH management, in which the supraphysiologic steroid doses needed to suppress adrenal androgens are themselves the cause of the growth failure, obesity and bone loss that follow. Reducing androgens by a route other than more steroid is the point.
practical: The clinically important variable is glucocorticoid dose reduction while androgen control holds — track both, not either alone. Note the evidence status: the two-year data are conference presentations, with the one-year results the peer-reviewed publication, and crinecerfont is FDA approved. Claims about BMI, metabolic risk and bone health follow from lowering steroid exposure but were not all demonstrated endpoints at two years.
link: Two-year CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) data in pediatric classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia

verify.status: corrected — one figure unverified and the evidence status overstated
verify.note: Real: two-year open-label extension data from the phase 3 CAHtalyst Pediatric study, 86 participants aged 4-17, durable ACTH and 17-OHP reductions with lower glucocorticoid doses, presented at the Pediatric Endocrine Society 2026 annual meeting with growth measures at ENDO 2026. THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) FIGURE NOT VERIFIED: the submission states a mean reduction of 3.2 mg/m²/day in glucocorticoid dosing. I could not confirm that number and it is not asserted; the confirmed finding is a sustained reduction to more physiologic dosing. (2) These are conference presentations, not a peer-reviewed two-year publication — the submission reads as though it were the latter. (3) 'Prompts major updates to pediatric endocrine society guidelines' could not be confirmed; FDA approval of crinecerfont is the verifiable anchor. The submission's list of downstream benefits (BMI, growth, metabolic risk, bone health) is mechanistically reasonable and growth measures were presented, but the full list was not all demonstrated at two years and is now framed accordingly.

title: Topical Berdazimer Gel 10.3% for Molluscum Contagiosum (B-SIMPLE4)
journal: JAMA Dermatology, with an integrated analysis in JAAD
breakthrough: B-SIMPLE4 was a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trial of berdazimer 10.3% gel, a topical nitric oxide donor, in 891 patients aged 6 months and over with 3 to 709 molluscum lesions, treated for 12 weeks with a further 12 weeks of safety follow-up. Complete clearance at week 12 was 32.4% with berdazimer versus 19.7% with vehicle (P < .0001), with an earlier gradient at week 8 (19.6% versus 11.6%) and week 4 (7.2% versus 3.6%). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 43.0%, 4.1% discontinued for one, and none were serious.
impact: The first prescription topical for molluscum, and an alternative to the two previous options: doing nothing, or a painful in-office destructive procedure on a young child.
practical: Set expectations from the actual numbers. About one child in three clears by 12 weeks on treatment against one in five on vehicle — an absolute difference of roughly 13 percentage points — so two thirds still have lesions at 12 weeks and the natural history is doing much of the work in both arms. That is still a reasonable trade for avoiding curettage or cantharidin, but it is not reliable clearance. Nearly half of treated children get a local adverse effect.
link: JAAD — berdazimer gel for molluscum contagiosum: integrated analysis of 3 randomized controlled trials

verify.status: corrected — efficacy overstated and the date is wrong by four years
verify.note: The trial is real with the numbers confirmed: B-SIMPLE4, 891 patients aged ≥6 months with 3-709 lesions, complete clearance 32.4% versus 19.7% vehicle at week 12 (P<.0001), week 8 19.6% versus 11.6%, week 4 7.2% versus 3.6%, TEAEs 43.0%, 4.1% discontinuation, none serious. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) EFFICACY: the submission says the gel 'reliably accelerating viral resolution' and achieved 'statistically significant complete clearance... with minimal localized side effects'. Statistically significant is right; reliable is not — two thirds of treated children had not cleared at 12 weeks, the absolute gain over vehicle is about 13 percentage points, and 43% had a treatment-emergent adverse event, which is not minimal. Both corrected, since this is exactly the entry a parent will be quoted. (2) DATE: B-SIMPLE4 was published in 2022 and berdazimer was FDA approved in January 2024 — it is not a 2026 development. The date field states this; the entry is left on the submitted year, as with other out-of-year citations in this project.

title: The 2026 AAP Immunization Schedule Diverges from the CDC Schedule
breakthrough: The AAP's 2026 schedule, released in Red Book Online, continues to recommend routine vaccination against 18 preventable diseases. The CDC schedule now covers 11. This ends a decades-long harmonisation between the two, which had produced a single national schedule. ACIP moved the infant hepatitis B recommendation, including the birth dose, from universal to shared clinical decision-making, and likewise moved COVID-19 vaccination; the AAP continues to recommend the hepatitis B birth dose within 24 hours of life plus subsequent doses at 1 to 2 months and 6 to 18 months, and continues to recommend COVID-19, RSV, rotavirus, influenza, hepatitis A and B and meningococcal vaccination. Twelve other national health organisations and 28 states have endorsed the AAP schedule rather than the CDC's.
impact: There is no longer one national childhood immunization schedule in the United States. Which document a clinician follows is now a choice with consequences for practice, for insurance coverage and for what a family is told.
practical: Know which schedule your institution, your state and your payers follow, because they may not agree. The hepatitis B birth dose is the sharpest divergence: the AAP position is universal administration within 24 hours to prevent perinatal transmission, while ACIP has made it a shared decision — and a missed birth dose is not recoverable in the infant who was exposed. Expect parents to arrive having read conflicting federal and professional guidance and to ask which is correct.
link: AAP News — the 2026 immunization schedule keeps routine recommendations intact after overhaul of the federal schedule

verify.status: REVERSED — the schedule's defining feature is divergence, not synchronisation
verify.note: The schedule is real (policy statement 26 January 2026, Pediatrics 157(3):e2025075754, Red Book Online, 18 diseases, hepatitis B within 24 hours of birth). THE FRAMING IS BACKWARDS ON THE POINT THAT MATTERS MOST. The submission says the AAP 'issued unified guidance', that it 'Reaffirms evidence-based national standards' and that it creates 'a synchronized clinical framework across primary care, obstetrics, and pediatric subspecialties'. In fact the 2026 schedule BROKE with the CDC: AAP covers 18 diseases to the CDC's 11, ending decades of harmonisation, after ACIP moved infant hepatitis B (including the birth dose) and COVID-19 vaccination from universal to shared clinical decision-making. Twelve other national organisations and 28 states have endorsed the AAP schedule over the CDC's. Describing this as synchronised national guidance would leave a resident unaware that two conflicting schedules exist, which is now a routine clinical and consent problem. Rewritten around the divergence, with the hepatitis B birth dose called out because it is the difference with the least recoverable consequence. The submission's co-sponsor list (AAFP, PIDS, ACOG, NAPNAP) is not asserted as I could not confirm it for this edition.

title: Exa-cel Gene Editing in Children Aged 5 to 11 with Sickle Cell Disease or Beta-Thalassemia
breakthrough: The CLIMB THAL-141 and CLIMB SCD-151 trials extended exagamglogene autotemcel to children aged 5 to 11. All children with sufficient follow-up met the primary endpoint: none with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia required a transfusion after the 60-day washout period, and none with sickle cell disease had a vaso-occlusive crisis after infusion. Haemoglobin normalised and safety was consistent with the older cohorts. These results contributed to the FDA expanding the approval to children aged 2 and over, from the previous limit of 12.
impact: Moves a potentially curative therapy in front of the complications it is meant to prevent. Silent cerebral infarction, vasculopathy and organ damage accumulate through childhood, and a therapy first available at 12 arrives after some of that is irreversible.
practical: The referral question changes: a young child with severe disease and no matched sibling donor is now a candidate, and the conversation should happen before end-organ damage rather than after. Two things must be in it — myeloablative busulfan conditioning, with veno-occlusive disease a recognised risk, and fertility preservation, which has to be addressed before conditioning in a child who cannot consent for themselves.
link: NEJM — exa-cel in children with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia or sickle cell disease

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, and the label expansion goes further than stated
verify.note: Verified: NEJMoa2603387, PMID 42274009, published online 10 June 2026; CLIMB THAL-141 and CLIMB SCD-151 in children aged 5-11; all patients with sufficient follow-up met the primary endpoint, with no transfusions after the 60-day washout in thalassaemia and no vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease; haemoglobin normalised; safety consistent with prior studies. TWO ADDITIONS. (1) The FDA has expanded approval to children aged 2 and over — a wider expansion than the 5-to-11 cohort studied, and the most consequential fact in the entry, which the submission omits entirely. (2) Busulfan-related veno-occlusive disease is named as the specific recognised risk; the submission refers to conditioning generically. The submission's points about referral before irreversible end-organ damage and about fertility preservation are sound and are kept. Kept as a separate entry from the 2025 long-term follow-up entry because this is a different age cohort in different trials that drove a label change, on the same basis as the OTOF durability entry in otolaryngology.

title: CONSORT-C 2026 and SPIRIT-C 2026: Reporting Standards for Paediatric Trials
journal: The BMJ, JAMA Pediatrics and The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health
breakthrough: Co-published across three journals, these extensions address the fact that trial reporting standards were built with adults in mind. SPIRIT-C 2026 adds 17 new items to SPIRIT 2025 for paediatric trial protocols; CONSORT-C 2026 adds 13 new items for reports. They cover age-appropriate outcomes and intervention delivery, consent and assent, family involvement and developmental needs. The work was led at SickKids by Ami Baba and Martin Offringa with 38 international co-authors — and notably, four SPIRIT-C items were generated by young people themselves and six more were youth-endorsed, with several CONSORT-C items rooted in priorities identified by children and caregivers.
impact: The youth-generated items are the genuinely new thing. Reporting standards have always been written by researchers about participants; here the participants specified what should be reported about them.
practical: For anyone designing or appraising a paediatric trial, these are the checklists to work from, and they are the reason future paediatric guidelines should rest less on extrapolated adult data. When reading an older paediatric trial, the new items double as a list of what was probably not reported.
link: The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health — CONSORT-Children and Adolescents (CONSORT-C) 2026 extension statement

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, one journal and the youth role added
verify.note: Verified: SPIRIT-C 2026 and CONSORT-C 2026 co-published February 2026, led at SickKids by Ami Baba and Martin Offringa with 38 international experts, covering age-appropriate outcomes and intervention delivery, consent and assent, family involvement and developmental needs. THREE ADDITIONS. (1) Co-publication includes JAMA Pediatrics as well as The BMJ and The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health; the submission names only two. (2) The item counts — 17 new SPIRIT-C items, 13 new CONSORT-C items — give the reader a sense of scale. (3) Most substantively, four SPIRIT-C items were youth-generated and six youth-endorsed, with CONSORT-C items rooted in priorities from children and caregivers. That is the distinctive feature of these extensions and the submission misses it entirely. ONE OMISSION: the submission's 'age-stratified subgroup analyses' could not be confirmed as a specific item and is not asserted.

title: Antibiotic Stewardship in Children and the WHO AWaRe Framework
breakthrough: The WHO AWaRe classification sorts antibiotics into Access (narrow-spectrum first-line agents with lower resistance risk), Watch (broad-spectrum agents needing restraint) and Reserve (last-line drugs for multidrug-resistant infection). An eClinicalMedicine study compared 80 national paediatric treatment guidelines for primary-care infections against the WHO AWaRe book recommendations. Point-prevalence surveys show wide variation in how much paediatric prescribing comes from the Access group — 74.8% at one quaternary hospital in Mozambique, but below target at a large children's hospital in London — with earlier global work finding paediatric Access proportions ranging from 7.8% in China to 61.2% in Slovenia.
impact: The variation is the finding. The same childhood respiratory infections are treated with narrow-spectrum agents in one health system and broad-spectrum ones in another, and the difference tracks local habit rather than local resistance.
practical: High-dose amoxicillin or penicillin remains first-line for routine otitis media, sinusitis and community-acquired pneumonia in a child, and second- or third-generation cephalosporins and macrolides are the substitutions worth auditing. Get the target right: the WHO 60% Access figure was a NATIONAL, all-ages target for 2023, not a paediatric benchmark, and the 79th UN General Assembly high-level meeting on AMR has since raised it to 70% of all human antibiotic use.
link: eClinicalMedicine — antibiotic treatment of pediatric infections in primary healthcare: comparison of 80 national guidelines with WHO AWaRe recommendations

verify.status: corrected — the cited study was not found and the target is wrong twice over
verify.note: The AWaRe framework and the over-reliance on Watch antibiotics in children are real, and the clinical advice (high-dose amoxicillin or penicillin first-line for otitis media, sinusitis and pneumonia) is sound and standard. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) THE TARGET IS WRONG IN TWO WAYS. The submission says the work 'setting a benchmark of at least 60% total pediatric antibiotic usage originating from the narrow-spectrum Access category'. The 60% Access figure is a WHO NATIONAL target covering all ages for 2023, not a paediatric-specific benchmark, and the 79th UNGA high-level meeting on AMR has raised it to 70%. A stewardship programme auditing paediatric prescribing against a 60% paediatric target would be measuring against a number that does not exist. (2) The specific study described — 'a major international study published in The Lancet' analysing global paediatric prescribing patterns — was not found. A closely related Lancet-family paper does exist (eClinicalMedicine, 80 national paediatric guidelines against the WHO AWaRe book) and has been substituted, together with the point-prevalence figures that show the actual variation.

title: Dual-AAV OTOF Gene Therapy for Congenital Auditory Neuropathy: The Paediatric Screening Consequence
breakthrough: Dual adeno-associated virus vector gene therapy delivering functional human OTOF into the inner ear has restored auditory function and speech perception in children with profound inherited deafness from otoferlin deficiency, with multicentre follow-up now extending to 2.5 years and treatment reported in patients as old as adolescence and young adulthood.
impact: For general paediatrics the significance is upstream of the ear. A treatable monogenic cause of profound congenital deafness means that a failed newborn hearing screen is now a trigger for genetic testing, not only for audiological follow-up.
practical: The practical demand is speed of diagnosis: identifying an OTOF variant early enough matters because auditory pathway development is time-sensitive, and candidacy depends on genotype. Two cautions belong with the enthusiasm — OTOF deafness is a small fraction of congenital hearing loss, so the great majority of deaf children remain cochlear implant candidates, and these are small single-arm trials rather than comparisons against implantation. Otolaryngology carries the fuller account of the trial data; this entry is the paediatric screening consequence.
link: Nature — multicentre gene therapy for OTOF-related deafness followed up to 2.5 years

verify.status: matched with corrections — real, and deliberately scoped to the paediatric angle
verify.note: Verified in the otolaryngology review of the same development: dual-AAV1 OTOF gene therapy, first-in-human restoration of hearing and speech perception published in Nature Medicine 2024, multicentre durability to 2.5 years in Nature 2026, age range extended beyond young children. TWO CORRECTIONS carried over. The construct is a DUAL-AAV vector, since the OTOF coding sequence exceeds single-AAV packaging capacity — the submission gets this right where earlier lists did not. And 'Rewrites pediatric otolaryngology and audiology guidelines, establishing targeted gene replacement as a viable alternative or adjunct to cochlear implants' overstates it: no guideline establishes this, and the population is a small minority of congenital hearing loss, so the entry says so. CROSS-SPECIALTY DUPLICATION, deliberate: this development also appears under otolaryngology for both years. It is kept here because the paediatric action — genetic testing triggered by a failed newborn hearing screen — is a different clinical behaviour from the otologist's, and the entry is written to the screening consequence rather than repeating the trial data. Same basis as the MeVO trials appearing in both emergency medicine and neurology.
